badges.name: American Business
badges.summary: Learn how business works in the United States, from free enterprise and finance to ethics and labor law, then research a business and explore a business career.

requirements.summary: Explore free enterprise and the history and reach of American business.

children.summary: Explain four features of U.S. free enterprise, how freedom differs from license, and how the Scout Oath and Law apply to business.
Describe the Industrial Revolution and the developments that began America's modern industrial era, and discuss three people who shaped U.S. business or industry and what each did.
Name and describe the five primary areas of business.
Trace the history of American labor unions, explain why unions and employers should cooperate, and name two major unions today.
Discuss how business affects the economy at local, national and global levels.

requirements.summary: Learn how businesses track, raise and protect money.

children.summary: Explain the income statement, balance sheet and statement of cash flows, and discuss how each guides business leaders' decisions.
Explain how changing interest rates, taxes and government spending push money toward or away from business and industry.
Explain how sole proprietorships, partnerships and LLCs raise capital, and four ways corporations do.
Name five kinds of insurance a business can use, and what each is for.

requirements.summary: Look at profit, sustainability, ethics and online selling.

children.summary: Explain the role profit plays in a business.
Describe green marketing and sustainable business practices.
Explain how ethics shapes business decisions.
Discuss how running a brick-and-mortar business differs from running one online.

requirements.summary: Describe what the U.S. Department of Labor does, and discuss two of these laws: FLSA, OSHA, FMLA and ERISA.
Pick a business, research how accounting, finance, economics, marketing and management each apply to it, and share what you find.
Explore a business career.

children.summary: Find three careers in one primary area of business, research one's education, training and experience, and discuss why it interests you.
Interview a business leader about their company and career path, discuss the role of ethics in business decisions, and share what you learned.

badges.name: American Cultures
badges.summary: Pick three groups with different racial, cultural, national or ethnic backgrounds, one of them your own, learn about them for requirements 1–3, and lead a discussion on how groups can understand one another.

requirements.summary: Learn about two of your groups, a different one for each choice.

children.summary: Attend a festival, celebration or other event of one group, then report on it.
Visit a place of worship, school or other institution of one group, then report on it.
Interview someone from one group about its heritage and traditions, then report on it.
Learn one group's traditional song, dance, poem or story, and teach it to some friends.
See a library or museum program or exhibit on one group's traditions, then report on it.

requirements.summary: Imagine a city or country where only one of your groups has ever lived; describe it today, then with all three of your groups living there.
Tell how your three groups' religious and social customs differ, and some ideas and practices they have in common.
Pick three people of different racial, ethnic or religious backgrounds, and tell your counselor how each has contributed to our country.
requirements.ownWork: Tell your counselor how the three people contributed to our country.

requirements.summary: Give your Scout unit or a school class a talk on how different groups have learned to live together, then lead a discussion on what would help groups understand each other.

badges.name: American Heritage
badges.summary: Explore the Declaration of Independence, people and groups who shaped the country, its national symbols, your family's and community's history, and how the past bears on today.

requirements.summary: Rewrite the Declaration of Independence's passage from "We hold these truths to be self-evident" to "new Guards for their future security" in plain words, then share it and discuss why the Declaration matters to all Americans.
Learn about America through its people and groups in two of these ways.

children.summary: Research a political leader and a private citizen from American history, and compare what each contributed to America's heritage.
With your counselor's approval, pick a group that brought positive change to American society, find out why and how it worked for that change, and discuss how it ties to America's past.
With your counselor's approval, interview two U.S. military veterans about what serving was like and what they think it achieved.
With your counselor's approval, interview three local people of different ages and jobs about what America means to them, what's special about it and which traditions to keep.

requirements.summary: Connect America's past with today.

children.summary: Pick a current news topic about the United States, describe what's happening, and explain how America's past events and values bear on it.

Describe how each of these was adopted, any changes since, and how it still influences Americans: the flag, the Pledge of Allegiance, the Great Seal of the United States, the motto and the national anthem.
Research your family's history and how events in American history touched it, including why they came to America if they immigrated, and share what you learn.

requirements.summary: Explore local history in two of these ways.

children.summary: Explain what the National Register of Historic Places is and how properties get listed, then map your area's points of historic interest and describe them, including any listed properties, to your counselor.
Research a historic event in or near your area, visit the site if you can, and tell how it shaped local history and how the place has changed since.
Trace your town or neighborhood's beginnings and the ethnic, national or racial groups involved, see how it has changed in the last 50 years, and explain why if you can.
Take on a role in a program about a person or event from America's past, then describe the program, what you did and what it covered.
Visit a historic trail or walk in your area, share what you learned, and discuss why the place matters and why it might qualify for the National Register.

requirements.summary: Look at history through film, a biography or music in one of these ways.

children.summary: With permission and approval, watch two movies set in American history and describe how accurately each shows its events and characters.

With your counselor's approval, read a biography of someone who contributed to America's heritage, tell what you do and don't admire about them, and explain whether their contribution was positive or negative and why.
Listen to popular songs from across American history, then share five and explain what each says about how people felt in its day; bring the lyrics if you can't play a recording.

requirements.summary: Explore careers in American heritage, and explain how to prepare for one that interests you, including the education and training it needs.

badges.name: American Indian Culture
badges.summary: Study American Indian cultural areas and one tribe or nation in depth, learn about languages, leaders and games, then visit a museum collection or a gathering. Formerly Indian Lore.

requirements.summary: Name the American Indian cultural areas and what sets each one apart.
Research a tribe, group or nation, then tell your counselor about each listed part of its life, past and present.
Learn about American Indian languages, place names and leaders.

children.summary: Learn 10 words in an American Indian language and what they mean.
Find out what 10 US place names of American Indian origin mean.
Name five notable American Indian leaders, past or present, with their tribes or nations and why each stands out.

requirements.summary: Look at how American Indians have shaped others' lives, and share a traditional game.

children.summary: Describe how European settlers would have fared without Native Americans already living here.
Describe eight things others took up from American Indians.
Learn a tribe's or group's game, then teach it to Scouts and lead them in playing it.

requirements.summary: Visit American Indian museum exhibits, in person or online, or a present-day gathering.

children.summary: Visit a museum in person or online, discuss two American Indian exhibitions, and identify 10 artifacts by tribe or nation, shape, size and use.
Go to a present-day American Indian gathering, then discuss its etiquette and what you saw and learned with your counselor.

badges.name: American Labor
badges.summary: Learn what concerns American workers, how unions and labor relations work and how the labor movement grew, and argue a labor issue from both sides.

requirements.summary: Research the concerns of working people, and list at least eight, describing each or giving examples.
With permission and approval, visit or contact a union, central labor council or employee organization, then do these.
requirements.ownWork: With permission and approval, visit the office or a meeting of a local union, central labor council or employee organization, or reach one online.

children.summary: Learn what the organization does.
Share your list of concerns from requirement 1, and ask which matter most to them and why.
Diagram how the organization is set up, from local to national level if it applies.

requirements.summary: Explain what unions are, what they do and how they serve members, showing you understand labor, management, collective bargaining, negotiation, union and open shops, grievance procedures, mediation, arbitration, work stoppages, strikes and lockouts.
Compare the adversarial model of labor-management relations with a cooperative-bargaining style.
Explore the labor movement's history in one of these ways.

children.summary: Make a timeline of key moments in American labor history, from the 1770s to now.
With an exhibit, scrapbook or computer presentation, show three big wins of the American labor movement and what they mean for workers.
With permission and approval, watch a movie about organized labor in the U.S., then discuss it and what you learned.
Read a biography, approved by your counselor, of someone who shaped the American labor movement, and explain their contribution.

requirements.summary: Explain globalization, how it affects American workers, and how the global workforce fits into the U.S. economy.

Pick a labor issue that matters to many workers, argue management's side and then labor's, aloud or in writing, and sum up the basic rights and responsibilities of employers and of union and nonunion employees.

Discuss the goals of a business's owners, stockholders, customers, employees, employee representatives, community and public officials, why they reach agreements and compromises, and how those affect each group.
Explore labor relations careers, pick one that interests you, and discuss its main duties and the qualifications, education and training it takes.

badges.name: Animal Science
badges.summary: Learn livestock breeds, diseases, digestion, management and breeding, then study beef cattle, dairy, horses, sheep or goats, hogs or poultry in depth.

requirements.summary: Name two breeds in each livestock class (horses, dairy cattle, beef cattle, sheep, hogs, poultry and goats), and tell your counselor their main uses, merits and origins.
requirements.ownWork: Tell your counselor each breed's main uses, merits and origins.

requirements.summary: List two diseases for each class in requirement 1, and describe to your counselor each one's symptoms, how animals catch it and how to prevent it.
requirements.ownWork: Describe the diseases to your counselor.

requirements.summary: Draw models of the digestive tracts of ruminants, horses, pigs and poultry, and explain how their differences shape each one's feeding.

Pick a beef cow, dairy cow, horse, sheep, goat, hog or poultry flock, and tell how you'd manage it, covering feeding, housing, disease prevention, waste removal, breeding and biosecurity as they apply.
Learn how livestock is bred and improved.

children.summary: Explain how producers improve their stock through breeding.
Explain pure breeding and cross breeding.
Give two modern technologies producers use with horses, dairy cattle, beef cattle, sheep, hogs, poultry or goats, and what each one offers.

requirements.summary: Complete one option to study a kind of livestock in depth.

children.summary: Option A: beef cattle.

Visit a beef farm or ranch, ask the operator how cattle are handled, fed, weighed and shipped, and report what you saw and learned; if you can't, use a breed association video or, with permission, online research.

Sketch either a feedlot for 30 or more fattening steers, with forage and grain storage and a loading chute, or a corral that handles 50 or more beef cows and their calves at once, with cutting and loading chutes.
Sketch the main wholesale and retail cuts of beef, and explain the USDA's dual grading system and the basis of each grade.
Define bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette and calf.
Option B: dairy.
Explain how a cow or goat makes milk from forage and grain, and how dairy and beef cows' feeds differ.
Chart the components of cow's or goat's milk and how much of each.
Explain what producing grade A milk takes, and why and how milk gets pasteurized.
Describe dairy farm milking equipment and the sanitation standards farms must meet.
Define bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe and kid.
Visit a dairy farm or milk processing plant and report what you saw and learned; if you can't, use a breed or dairy association video or, with permission, online research.
Option C: horse.
Sketch a practical barn and exercise yard for saddle horses.
Tell the horse's history and how it has helped people, and discuss the special uses of each horse breed you chose in requirement 1.
Define mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo and tobiano.
Visit a horse farm and report what you saw and learned; if you can't, use a breed association video or, with permission, online research.
Outline how to feed a horse doing light work and why feed changes with the horse and its work, and describe colic, its causes and symptoms.
Option D: sheep or goat (pick one).
Sketch a live lamb or goat, marking where its wholesale and retail cuts are.
Discuss how wool is sorted and graded.
List products made from the milk.
Raise an animal or visit a farm.
Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight, keeping records of its feed, weight gain, medication, vaccinations and any deaths for your counselor to review.
Visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch and report what you saw and learned; if you can't, use a breed association video or, with permission, online research.
Define wether, ewe, ram and lamb for sheep, or doe, nanny, kid, buck and billy for goats.
Option E: hog.
Sketch the main wholesale and retail cuts of pork, and explain the recommended USDA pork grades and the basis of each.
Write an outline of feeding a gilt or sow from breeding through weaning the litter, and discuss feeding during growth and finishing.
Raise a pig or visit a hog operation.
Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight, keeping records of its feed, weight gain, medication, vaccinations and any deaths for your counselor to review.
Visit a hog farm or packing plant and report what you saw and learned; if you can't, use a packer or processor video or, with permission, online research.
Define gilt, sow, barrow and boar.
Option F: avian.

Sketch a layer or broiler house with nests, roosts, feeders, waterers and ventilation; explain how environmental controls keep birds safe in heat, cold and bad weather, and why light matters for egg production.
Explain the dangers of overcrowding a poultry flock.
Explain how eggs are graded and what the classes of chicken meat are.
Raise poultry or visit a producer.
Manage a laying flock for five months, keeping records of feed bought, eggs sold, medication, vaccinations and deaths for your counselor to review.
Raise five chickens from hatching, keeping records of their feed, weight gain, medication, vaccinations and deaths for your counselor to review.
Visit a commercial poultry facility and report what you saw and learned; if you can't, use a poultry association video or, with permission, online research.
Define chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock and capon.

requirements.summary: Explore three animal science careers, research one's education, training and experience, and discuss why it might interest you.

badges.name: Animation
badges.summary: Learn what animation is, how it began and what makes it believable, then make animations with two techniques.

requirements.summary: Learn what animation is and where it came from.

children.summary: Explain animation in your own words.
Discuss how animation began and developed.

requirements.summary: Explain how five of the 12 listed animation principles make motion more convincing.
With your counselor's approval, pick two animation techniques and make an animation with each.

children.summary: Make an animation with your first technique.
Work out your animation first in thumbnail sketches or layout drawings, on paper or in software.
Make the animation.
Present it to your counselor, walk through your process, and talk about how to improve it.
Make an animation with your second technique.
Work out your animation first in thumbnail sketches or layout drawings.
Make the animation.
Present it to your counselor, walk through your process, and talk about how to improve it.

requirements.summary: See how animation is used in the world.

children.summary: Tour an animation studio or business, in person or online, and report what you learned.
Discuss how animation might someday help you have more fun and get more done.

requirements.summary: Explore three animation careers, research one, and discuss why it might interest you.

badges.name: Archaeology
badges.summary: Learn how archaeologists find, date and interpret sites, study sites at home and abroad and people who once lived near you, help protect the past, and try fieldwork or a mock dig.

requirements.summary: Explain what archaeology is and how it compares with anthropology, geology, paleontology, history, artifact collecting and treasure hunting.

Describe each step of archaeological work: site location, background research and research design, survey and fieldwork, artifact identification and examination, interpretation, preservation and sharing information.
Describe two or more ways archaeologists date sites, structures or artifacts, and explain absolute and relative dating.
Learn about five archaeological sites in all, some in the United States and some elsewhere.

children.summary: For each site, locate it on a map, tell how archaeologists learned of it, what it reveals and why that matters to archaeologists and people today; then compare the sites' ages.
children.ownWork: Compare how old the five sites are.

columns.label: What it reveals about the past

children.summary: Give a short talk on one of the sites to a Cub Scout pack, your troop, your class or another group.

requirements.summary: Learn how archaeological sites are protected.

children.summary: Learn the federal laws and international agreements that protect archaeological sites, and whether your state, county or local government has rules for archaeological or historic sites.
Find a national, international or local group that works to safeguard archaeological sites.

requirements.summary: Learn how to help protect the past.

children.summary: Explain why archaeological sites need protecting.
Explain what to do if you think you've found an artifact.
Describe ways you can help protect the past.

requirements.summary: Do one of these and discuss what you found with your counselor.
requirements.ownWork: Discuss your findings with your counselor.

children.summary: Visit a museum and see how its artifacts help tell history.
Share a meaningful family heirloom or artifact with your counselor and talk about its history.
List the trash your family throws away in a week, and discuss what archaeologists a thousand years from now might learn about your family from it.

requirements.summary: Research a group that called your area home over a century ago: their way of life, ties to other groups, what you'd expect at one of their sites and how they shaped your community.
Research a career related to archaeology and discuss what makes it interesting.
Do archaeology hands-on in one of these ways.

children.summary: With permission and approval, help a qualified archaeologist on a project for at least eight hours, following their safety rules, then describe your part, what you learned and the steps of archaeological inquiry.

With your counselor's approval, join a mock dig set up by a qualified archaeologist: analyze and map its artifacts and features, explain how environment and time affect what they tell us, and how you'd share results.

requirements.summary: Do one of these with a qualified archaeologist or instructor supervising.

children.summary: Help set up a public archaeology display, such as at a museum, visitor center or school.
Try experimental archaeology by remaking an object or practicing a skill from the past, then write a short report on what you did and found.

badges.name: Archery
badges.summary: Learn range safety and arrow care, then shoot a recurve, longbow or compound bow for score.

requirements.summary: Learn to stay safe on the archery range.

children.summary: Explain why anything that fires a projectile needs care and the right place.
Explain the five rules of range safety.
Explain what the four range whistle signals mean.
Show how to pull arrows from the target safely and put them away.
Explain the laws where you live for owning and using archery gear.

requirements.summary: Learn about arrows.

children.summary: Identify the parts of an arrow.
Describe at least three kinds of arrows.
Name the four main materials arrow shafts are made of.
Make or repair arrows.
Build a full arrow from a bare shaft.
Replace at least three vanes, a point and a nock on arrows.
Explain how to care for and store arrows.

requirements.summary: Learn about archery gear and terms.

children.summary: Explain how to use, care for and store tabs, arm guards, gloves and quivers.
Explain draw length, draw weight, mechanical release and barebow.

requirements.summary: Explain how archery is organized and scored.

children.summary: How an end differs from a round.
How field, target and 3-D archery differ.
How to score the five-color World Archery target.
How to score NFAA field and indoor targets.

requirements.summary: With a certified instructor, complete one bow option.

children.summary: Option A: recurve bow or longbow.
Identify the parts of your bow.
Explain how to care for and store a recurve bow or longbow.
Walk your counselor through USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting with your bow.
Show how to string a recurve bow or longbow.
Find and mark the nocking point on your bowstring with a bow square.
Shoot for a qualifying score.
Shoot one round with a finger release and reach its score.
NFAA field round: 60 points.
Scouting America field round: 80 points.
World Archery or USA Archery indoor round: 80 points.
NFAA indoor round: 50 points.
Shoot 30 arrows at 10 yards for 150 points on a five-color target.
Option B: compound bow.
Identify the parts of your bow.
Explain how to care for and store a compound bow.
Walk your counselor through USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting with your bow.
Explain why a compound bow's string or cable is replaced at a shop.
Find and mark the nocking point on your bowstring.
Shoot for a qualifying score.
Shoot one round with a finger release and reach its score.
NFAA field round: 70 points.
Scouting America field round: 90 points.
World Archery or USA Archery indoor round: 90 points.
NFAA indoor round: 60 points.
Shoot 15 arrows at 10 yards and 15 at 15 yards for 160 points.

badges.name: Architecture
badges.summary: Study the buildings around you and a landmark of architecture, learn about sustainable design, meet with an architect or a future client, and draw a room's floor plan to scale.

requirements.summary: Look at architecture around you and in history.

children.summary: Tour your community, note the kinds of buildings you see and any you can tie to a period of history or style, and sketch the one you admire most.
Pick a historic achievement in architecture that changed society, research its influence on today's world in books, magazines or online (with permission), and tell your counselor what you learned.

requirements.summary: Discuss these ideas about architecture and the environment, in the spirit of Leave No Trace and the Outdoor Code.

children.summary: What sustainable architecture means, and three features green buildings usually have.
How renewable and recycled building materials differ, and ways to build with each.
How architecture relates to its surroundings and its community.
Finding a new use for a whole building once its first use ends, instead of tearing it down.

requirements.summary: Meet with an architect or a future client in one of these ways.

children.summary: With permission and approval, meet an architect, look at a building's scale model and construction drawings, and discuss why its materials were chosen and how its parts are joined.

With your parent or guardian's, counselor's, architect's and site manager's permission, visit a construction site with an architect and the builder's drawings; follow its safety rules and discuss why its materials were chosen and how they're joined.
Interview a possible client, such as someone planning a home or business, about what their new building must do, and write a short program of its requirements, functions, how they relate and goals.

requirements.summary: Measure a room and draw its floor plan at ¼ inch = 1 foot, showing walls, doors, closets, windows and built-ins, labeled with your name, the date, the room and the scale.
Explore three architecture careers, research one, and discuss why it might interest you.

badges.name: Art
badges.summary: Learn the elements and principles of art, work in several media, and explore art careers.

requirements.summary: Talk with your counselor about what art is.

children.summary: Explain what art is and name some of its forms.
Explain why art matters to people.
Describe your own connection to art and the feelings it gives you.

requirements.summary: Explain line, value, shape, form, space, color and texture, with an example of each.
Discuss rhythm, balance, proportion, variety, emphasis and unity, the six design principles.
Draw or paint one subject in four different media.

children.summary: Pen and ink.
Watercolors.
Pencil.
Pastels.
Oil paints.
Tempera.
Acrylics.
Charcoal.
Drawing or painting on a computer.

requirements.summary: Do one design or storytelling project.

children.summary: Design a useful item, sketch or model it, and promote it with pictures.
Tell a story in pictures or a 3-D rendering.
Design a logo, explain what it means, and put it on something, with permission.

requirements.summary: Visit a museum, gallery, exhibit, artists' co-op or workshop, and discuss what you learned.
Explore three art careers and the training one of them needs.

badges.name: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
badges.summary: Learn what AI and automation are and how they're used, weigh AI's ethics and risks such as deepfakes, practice working with AI, and put it to use in a project or lesson.

requirements.summary: Explain what each of these terms means: artificial intelligence (AI), AI agents, automation, basic programming, bots, data, databases, digital workers, general AI, machine learning (ML), narrow AI, superintelligent AI, tasks, triggers, workflows and variables.
Learn the basics of AI, and share what you learned.
requirements.ownWork: Share what you learned with your counselor.

children.summary: Give 10 examples of AI in everyday life today.
Give five examples of AI at work today.
Give five ways AI can help at school or with your education.
Play 10 rounds of the "AI or Not?" game with your counselor, deciding whether each scenario uses AI, and discuss your answers.
Make a timeline of five turning points in the history of AI.

requirements.summary: Learn the basics of automation, and share what you learned.
requirements.ownWork: Share what you learned with your counselor.

children.summary: Give 10 examples of automation in everyday life today.
Give five examples of automation at work today.
Give five ways automation can help at school or with your education.
Explain how automation runs repetitive tasks on its own, making fewer mistakes than people and using resources better.
Make a timeline of five turning points in the history of automation.

requirements.summary: Explore ethics in AI, and share what you learned.
requirements.ownWork: Share what you learned with your counselor.

children.summary: Research the ethics of AI and how to use it responsibly, including bias, privacy and decisions made by AI.
Play and discuss five rounds of the "What Would You Do?" ethics scenarios with your counselor.
Write your own rules for using AI ethically.
Explain the Turing test.

requirements.summary: Learn about deepfakes, and share what you learned.
requirements.ownWork: Share what you learned with your counselor.

children.summary: Explain what a deepfake is and how it can harm someone.
Describe what to do if a deepfake affects you or someone you know.

requirements.summary: Build skills for working with AI, and share what you learned.
requirements.ownWork: Share what you learned with your counselor.

children.summary: Discuss how AI learns and where it falls short.
Name five ways to communicate effectively with AI.
Explain why prompt engineering matters for getting better results from AI.
Give three examples of clear instructions you'd write for a school task.

requirements.summary: Put AI to work in one of these ways.

children.summary: With your counselor's approval, pick an AI project for an interest of yours or a community need, plan its goals, data needs and ethical issues, build it with suitable AI tools, and share it, the steps you took and how it went.

With your counselor's approval, plan and teach a short AI lesson to your patrol or other Scouts, including an age-appropriate AI-generated explanation of AI, everyday and workplace examples, and a hands-on demo of AI helping with schoolwork, Scouting or advancement; then share how you made and taught it.

requirements.summary: Explore an AI or automation career.

children.summary: Explore three AI or automation careers, research one, and discuss whether it interests you.

Interview an AI or automation professional about their daily work, challenges and view of the field's future, and the training, education, certifications, experience and costs to get started, and share what you learned.

badges.name: Astronomy
badges.summary: Learn to use telescopes and read the night sky, from constellations and planets to the Moon and Sun.

requirements.summary: Stay safe while doing astronomy.

children.summary: Explain astronomy hazards and how to prevent and handle them.
Explain first aid for heat, cold, dehydration, bites, stings and eye damage.
Describe what to wear and how to observe safely at night and in the cold.
Explain how to look at the Sun, things near it and solar eclipses without harm.

Learn about telescopes and binoculars, using diagrams or real ones.

Look at a planet and tell what you observed.

With diagrams, show where the Sun, Earth and Moon are during eclipses and phases.

children.summary: Describe the Sun's makeup, its place among stars, and its radiation's effects on Earth.
Define sunspots and explain how they can change the Sun's radiation.
Find red, blue and yellow stars other than the Sun, and explain the colors.

children.summary: Learn about local weather dangers and warnings from a weather service office or a weather expert.

requirements.summary: Give a counselor-approved talk of at least five minutes to a group on lightning, flash flood and tornado safety.
Research a career related to weather and discuss what makes it interesting.

badges.name: Welding
badges.summary: Learn to weld safely, set up your own welding process, and make basic welds and joints.

requirements.summary: Prepare to weld safely.

Describe welding safety gear, then show up dressed in it.
Show how to care for and store welding tools and protective gear.

Name cutting methods, then explain how to use one and its pros and cons.
Get ready to weld.

children.summary: List the equipment for two welding processes, and a pro and con of each.
Set up one process, and have your counselor approve the area.

requirements.summary: Practice welding with your setup, after finishing requirements 1 to 5.

children.summary: Draw your initial on a plate and weld a bead along it.
Cover a small plate with side-by-side beads.
Tack-weld two plates into a square groove butt joint.
Weld the butt joint from 6c on both sides.
Tack a T joint, have it checked, then fillet weld both sides.
Tack a lap joint, have it checked, then fillet weld both sides.

requirements.summary: Explore the welding profession.

children.summary: Explore three welding careers, research one, and discuss why it might interest you.
Discuss what the American Welding Society does for welders.

badges.name: Whitewater
badges.summary: Earn Canoeing or Kayaking first, then learn to paddle moving water safely: read rivers, signal, maneuver, make rescues, and plan and paddle whitewater trips.

requirements.summary: Learn whitewater safety.

children.summary: Explain likely whitewater hazards, including fallen trees, rocks, hydraulics at ledges or low-head dams, strong wind, cold, and thunderstorms, and how to anticipate, prevent, lessen and respond to them.

Discuss Safety Afloat and the American Whitewater safety guidelines, including helmets and life jackets.

requirements.summary: Learn how rivers and boats behave.

children.summary: Draw lines showing how water flows through an upstream V, downstream V, riffle, eddy and eddy line, ledge, river bend, shallows, current at different depths, drop, horizon line and hydraulic.
Explain what makes waves, including standing waves and wave trains.
Explain how to edge the boat while keeping your body upright.
Entering and leaving an eddy.
Ferrying downstream and upstream.
Explain when, why and how to scout a river from shore and from the water, and when to portage instead.

requirements.summary: Earn Canoeing or Kayaking, then show its strokes and maneuvers.
requirements.ownWork: Earn Canoeing or Kayaking, whichever matches the boat you'll use, before starting requirements 4 through 12.

children.summary: If you're using a canoe, show your counselor the strokes and maneuvers from Canoeing.
If you're using a kayak, show your counselor the strokes and maneuvers from Kayaking.

requirements.summary: On calm water, show the strokes and techniques for your kind of boat.

children.summary: Option A: tandem canoeist. Do all of these on calm water.

From the stern: stern draw, stern pry, sculling draw, and forward with stern pry.
High brace, low brace and righting pry.

Cross forward, bow draw, cross bow draw, stern draw, pry, stern pry, sculling draw, and forward with stern pry.
High brace, low brace and righting pry.
Option C: solo kayaker. Do all of these on calm water.
Bow draw, rudder and sculling draw.
High brace and low brace.

requirements.summary: Learn to rate a river's difficulty.

children.summary: Explain the International Scale of River Difficulty, and use it to rate a stretch of river your counselor approves.
Identify the features of that river that set its class on the scale.
Discuss how the amount of flow can move a river from one class to another and change its features and hazards.

requirements.summary: Explain why communication matters on every whitewater outing, and use the American Whitewater Universal River Signals, visual and audible, for stop, are you OK, help, run river right or left, and all clear.
Describe the boats paddled on moving water.

children.summary: If you're using a canoe, describe the kinds of moving-water canoes and how their design, materials and purpose differ.
If you're using a kayak, describe the kinds of moving-water kayaks and how their design, materials and purpose differ.

requirements.summary: Go over with your counselor the personal and group gear a safe whitewater outing calls for, and how and why to use each.
Read a Class II stretch of river your counselor approves: describe the best lines and other routes, how to use its features and how to stay clear of its hazards.
In a proper life jacket and dressed for the weather and water, do these on moving water in an equipped whitewater tandem canoe, solo canoe or solo kayak; in a tandem, do each from bow and stern.

children.summary: Launch and land.
Paddle straight ahead for at least 10 boat lengths.
Backpaddle straight for at least five boat lengths.
Ferry upstream from each side of the river.
Ferry downstream from each side of the river.
Do an eddy turn from each side of an eddy.
Peel out from each side of an eddy.

requirements.summary: Explain and show these to your counselor.

children.summary: Rescuing yourself after capsizing in moving water, including a wet exit if needed.
Using a throw rope to rescue a swimmer in whitewater.
Catching a throw rope as the swimmer.
Portaging: where it makes sense, and when and how to do it.
The whitewater buddy system, with at least three people in three boats.

requirements.summary: Paddle whitewater trips on Class I or II rivers, at least six hours in all, and do these for each trip.
requirements.ownWork: Paddle one or more canoe or kayak trips on a Class I or II river, with at least six hours of paddling in all.

children.summary: Help write the trip plan: route with put-ins and takeouts, schedule, gear, safety precautions and emergency procedures.
Find out the local rules and get permission from landowners and land managers ahead of time.
Explain how the trip follows Safety Afloat and the American Whitewater safety guidelines.
Show how to keep personal and group gear dry and how to load and secure it in the boats, then run the trip as planned with other paddlers.
Review with your counselor how your plans held up on each trip.

badges.name: Wilderness Survival
badges.summary: Learn to avoid and get through a survival situation: first aid, shelter, fire, signals and water.

requirements.summary: Learn backcountry hazards and first aid.

children.summary: Show or explain how to prevent and treat these backcountry problems.
Dehydration.
Heatstroke.
Hypothermia.
Shock.
Blisters.
Eye injuries.
Ankle and knee sprains.
Chigger, tick, mosquito and gnat bites.
Bee stings.
Spider bites.
Scorpion stings.
Wild mammal bites.
Venomous snakebites.
Describe how the Scout Basic Essentials help in a survival situation and a survival kit.
Explain how a trip plan can keep you out of a survival situation.

requirements.summary: Explain why each of the seven survival priorities matters.
Explain how to stay calm and upbeat when lost, and why it matters.
Assemble your own first-aid kit and survival kit, and show how to use them.
Learn to find shelter and stay protected.

children.summary: Describe how you'd survive in each of these conditions.
Cold and snow.
Wet.
Hot and dry.
Windy.
On the water or at its edge.
Show the right clothing for extreme heat, cold and wet weather.
Explain how to stay safe around bears and raccoons.
Describe forest and snow survival shelters you could build or find.
Build a low-impact natural shelter and spend a night in it.

requirements.summary: Build and light three fires, each a different way without matches.
Learn to signal for help.

children.summary: Explain and show how to signal ground, air or water searchers.
Show how to signal with a mirror.
From memory, describe and explain five ground-to-air signals.

requirements.summary: Show three ways to make outdoor water safe to drink.
Explain why eating wild plants or animals is usually unwise when lost.
Explore a career or hobby connected to wilderness survival.

children.summary: Research a related career and discuss what makes it interesting.
Research a related hobby or volunteer role, and set goals for it.

badges.name: Wildland Fire Management
badges.summary: Learn how wildfires behave, the harm they do and the good prescribed fire can do, how they're prevented and fought safely, and take action against wildfire where you live.

requirements.summary: Research and discuss the history of wildland fire in the U.S. and how it has been fought, prevented and managed.
Research the harm wildfires do in the U.S., including acres burned in each of the last three years, and discuss their effects on these.

children.summary: Commercial forest products.
Fish and wildlife habitat.
Soil and water.
Recreation and public use.
Homes, communities and human resources.
Air quality and public health.

Fish and wildlife habitat enhancement.
Ecosystem restoration.
Forest regeneration.
Insect and disease control.

The main causes of wildfires in the U.S.
How you can prevent human-caused wildfires in your community and on unit outings.
Wildfire mitigation.
The wildland-urban interface.
Defensible space, and how to protect homes and communities in the wildland-urban interface from wildfire.

Explain how removing heat, fuel or oxygen can put out a wildfire.
Diagram the parts of a wildfire.

The 10 Standard Firefighting Orders.
The 18 Watch Out Situations.
Lookouts, Communication, Escape Routes and Safety Zones (LCES).

Indirect attack.
Minimum impact suppression tactics.
Using hand crews, machinery and aircraft.
Mop-up.
Repair and restoration.

children.summary: Show how to use three hand tools made for wildland firefighting, and use one to build a fireline.

requirements.summary: Take action on wildfire in one of these ways.

V cut.
Stop cut or score line.

ranks.name: Scout

Explain how merit badges work and how to earn one.

requirements.summary: Learn more first aid and rescue skills, and prepare your home for emergencies.

children.summary: Bandage a sprained ankle and injuries to the head, upper arm and collarbone.
Show how to move a person out of a smoke-filled room and carry someone with a sprained ankle 25 yards or more, both alone and with a partner.
Name the five most common signs of a heart attack and explain the steps of CPR.
List the utilities in your home or meeting place, their hazards, and how to respond to emergencies with them.
Make a home emergency plan covering fire, storms, and power and water outages.
Explain how to get safe drinking water in an emergency.

requirements.summary: Stay active for four more weeks, and set a goal to keep it up.

children.summary: After Second Class 7a, get at least 30 minutes of activity a day, five days a week, for four more weeks, and log it.
Talk about what was hard and what went well in 8a, and set a goal to stay active every day.

requirements.summary: Learn about citizenship and the environment, and give three hours of service.

children.summary: Meet with someone your leader approves, such as an elected official, judge or teacher, to discuss a U.S. citizen's constitutional rights and duties.
Look into a local environmental issue, share what you learn with your patrol or troop, and say what you or your community could do.
Note the trash you make on an outing, then plan to reduce, recycle or repurpose what you bring on the next similar one, carry out the plan and compare.
Give three hours of service on Scoutmaster-approved projects not used for Tenderfoot 7b or Second Class 8e, and relate it to the Scout Law.

requirements.summary: Tell a possible new Scout or an inactive one about your Scouting, invite them to an event, tell them how to join or encourage them to come back, and report to an adult leader.
Live the Scout Oath and Law. Tell how you've done your duty to God and lived four points of the Law not used for earlier ranks.
Have a Scoutmaster conference for this rank, after the one for Second Class.
Pass your First Class board of review.

ranks.name: Star
ranks.summary: Earn six merit badges, and as a First Class Scout, serve in a troop leadership position for four months and give six hours of service.

requirements.summary: As a First Class Scout, take an active part in your troop for four months or more.
As a First Class Scout, live the Scout Oath and Law, and tell how you've done your duty to God and lived them day to day.
Earn six merit badges, at least four of them from the Eagle-required list.
As a First Class Scout, give six hours of service on Scoutmaster-approved projects.
As a First Class Scout, serve four months in troop positions of responsibility (not assistant patrol leader), or do a Scoutmaster-approved leadership project.
Learn about personal safety with your parent or guardian.

children.summary: With your parent or guardian, work through the exercises in How to Protect Your Children from Child Abuse: A Parent's Guide.
With permission, watch the Personal Safety Awareness videos.

requirements.summary: Have a Scoutmaster conference as a First Class Scout.
Pass your Star board of review.

ranks.name: Life
ranks.summary: Earn 11 merit badges in all, and as a Star Scout, lead in your troop for six months, give service that includes conservation, and teach another Scout.

requirements.summary: As a Star Scout, take an active part in your troop for six months or more.
As a Star Scout, live the Scout Oath and Law, and tell how you've done your duty to God and lived them day to day.
Earn five more merit badges for 11 in all, at least seven of them Eagle-required.
As a Star Scout, give six hours of service on Scoutmaster-approved projects, with at least three hours on conservation.
As a Star Scout, serve six months in troop positions of responsibility (not assistant patrol leader), or do a Scoutmaster-approved leadership project.
As a Star Scout, use Teaching EDGE to teach another Scout, ideally a younger one, the skills in one choice below, until they're ready to pass them to their Scoutmaster's satisfaction.

children.summary: Tenderfoot 4a and 4b (first aid).
Second Class 2b, 2c and 2d (cooking and tools).
Second Class 3a and 3d (navigation).
First Class 3a, 3b, 3c and 3d (tools).
First Class 4a and 4b (navigation).
Second Class 6a and 6b (first aid).
First Class 7a and 7b (first aid).
Three requirements from one Eagle-required merit badge, with your Scoutmaster's approval.

requirements.summary: Have a Scoutmaster conference as a Star Scout.
Pass your Life board of review.

ranks.name: Eagle Scout
ranks.summary: The highest rank. Earn 21 merit badges in all, and as a Life Scout, lead a service project and serve six months in a troop leadership position.

requirements.summary: As a Life Scout, take an active part in your troop for six months or more.
As a Life Scout, live the Scout Oath and Law, and tell how you've done your duty to God, lived them, and expect them to guide your future. List references on your Eagle Scout Rank Application.
Earn 21 merit badges in all, including the 13 required for Eagle. Extra badges from an either-or choice count as electives.
As a Life Scout, serve six months in troop positions of responsibility, not assistant patrol leader or bugler. A leadership project can't replace it.

As a Life Scout, plan, develop and lead a service project that helps a religious institution, school or your community, not Scouting America. Use the Eagle Scout Service Project Workbook, and get your proposal approved first by the organization it helps, your Scoutmaster and troop committee, and your council or district.
Have a Scoutmaster conference as a Life Scout.
Attach a statement of your ambitions and life purpose, and a list of leadership positions and honors, to your application, then pass your Eagle Scout board of review.
